q: Sattriya, one of the eight classical dances of India, belongs to which state?
x: Sattriya grew in the Vaishnava monasteries (sattras) of Assam founded by Srimanta Sankardeva in the 15th century. Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised it as a classical dance in 2000.
e: Sattriya comes from 'sattra', the Assamese monastery — the dance is named after the building it was born in.

q: Mohiniyattam, performed mainly by women as a solo dance, is the classical dance of which state?
x: Mohiniyattam is Kerala's classical dance. The name means 'dance of the enchantress' (Mohini, the female form of Vishnu); it uses gentle, swaying movements and a white-and-gold costume.
e: Kerala has two classical dances: Kathakali (dramatic, with painted faces) and Mohiniyattam (gentle, solo).

q: Which classical dance form takes its name from a village in Andhra Pradesh?
x: Kuchipudi is named after Kuchipudi village in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh. It mixes dance with spoken dialogue and is known for the tarangam, danced on the rim of a brass plate.
e: Kuchipudi = a village name; the dancer balancing on a brass plate is its signature.

q: Chhau, inscribed on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010, is NOT traditionally performed in which of these states?
x: Chhau is a masked martial dance of Odisha (Mayurbhanj), Jharkhand (Seraikella) and West Bengal (Purulia). Kerala's classical forms are Kathakali and Mohiniyattam instead.
e: Three Chhau styles, three states: Mayurbhanj (Odisha), Seraikella (Jharkhand), Purulia (West Bengal).

q: Rukmini Devi Arundale founded which institution for the revival of Bharatanatyam?
x: Rukmini Devi Arundale founded Kalakshetra at Adyar, Chennai, in 1936. She brought Bharatanatyam from temple courtyards onto the modern stage.
e: Kalakshetra = 'place of art'; Chennai, 1936, Rukmini Devi Arundale.

q: Ghoomar is a well-known folk dance of which state?
x: Ghoomar is a Rajasthani folk dance performed by women in flowing ghagras who move in a circle; the name comes from 'ghoomna', to twirl.
e: Ghoomar twirls in Rajasthan; Garba circles in Gujarat; Bhangra leaps in Punjab.

q: Pandit Shivkumar Sharma was the master of which musical instrument?
x: Shivkumar Sharma brought the santoor, a many-stringed Kashmiri folk instrument struck with wooden mallets, onto the Hindustani classical stage.
e: Santoor = Shivkumar Sharma; shehnai = Bismillah Khan; sarod = Amjad Ali Khan.

q: Which of the following is a percussion instrument?
x: The mridangam is the main percussion instrument of Carnatic music. The sitar is plucked, the sarangi is bowed and the bansuri is a wind instrument.
e: Mridangam is to Carnatic music what the tabla is to Hindustani music.

q: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri are together known as the trinity of which form of music?
x: These three 18th-19th century composers are called the Trinity of Carnatic music; between them they wrote much of its core repertoire.
e: All three were born in Thiruvarur, Tamil Nadu — the Carnatic trinity from one town.

q: The Hornbill Festival, held every December, is celebrated in which state?
x: The Hornbill Festival is held at Kisama near Kohima, Nagaland, every December. It brings together the major Naga tribes and is called the 'Festival of Festivals'.
e: The hornbill — the bird whose feathers appear in Naga headgear — gives Nagaland's festival its name.

q: Pongal, a four-day harvest festival, is chiefly celebrated in which state?
x: Pongal is the Tamil harvest festival held in mid-January, when freshly harvested rice is boiled in milk until it overflows — a sign of plenty.
e: Same season, different names: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Makar Sankranti (north), Magh Bihu (Assam), Lohri (Punjab).

q: Onam, the harvest festival associated with the legendary King Mahabali, is celebrated in which state?
x: Onam is Kerala's ten-day harvest festival in the month of Chingam, marking the yearly homecoming of King Mahabali. It features the Vallam Kali snake-boat race and the Onasadya feast.
e: Onam: flower carpets (pookalam), snake boats and a feast served on a banana leaf.

q: The Khajuraho group of temples was built by which dynasty?
x: The Khajuraho temples in Madhya Pradesh were built by the Chandela rulers between about 950 and 1050 CE. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
e: Khajuraho = Chandelas = Madhya Pradesh, built in the nagara style.

q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved out of a single rock, was built under which dynasty?
x: The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) at Ellora was carved downwards out of one basalt hill during the reign of the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century.
e: Ellora's Kailasa was cut from the hilltop down — the largest monolithic excavation in the world.

q: The Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur was built by which ruler?
x: Rajaraja Chola I completed the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur in 1010 CE. It is one of the 'Great Living Chola Temples' on the UNESCO list.
e: Rajaraja built Thanjavur; his son Rajendra built Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

q: The Charminar in Hyderabad was built by which ruler?
x: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built the Charminar in 1591, when Hyderabad was founded. Its name means 'four minarets'.
e: Char (four) + minar (tower) — Quli Qutb Shah, 1591, Hyderabad.

q: The Hawa Mahal in Jaipur was built by which ruler?
x: Sawai Pratap Singh built the Hawa Mahal in 1799; it was designed by Lal Chand Ustad. Its many small windows let royal women watch street processions unseen.
e: Hawa Mahal = 'palace of winds' — a five-storey screen of 953 jharokhas.

q: The Rajatarangini, a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, was written by whom?
x: Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini in Sanskrit in the 12th century. It is often called India's earliest work of proper historical writing.
e: Rajatarangini = 'river of kings'; Kalhana, Kashmir, 12th century.

q: Who wrote the Harshacharita, a biography of King Harshavardhana?
x: Banabhatta was Harshavardhana's court poet and wrote both the Harshacharita and the romance Kadambari.
e: Bana wrote the life of his own patron Harsha — a court poet writing the king's story.

q: The Ain-i-Akbari was written by whom?
x: Abul Fazl, one of Akbar's nine gems, wrote the Akbarnama; the Ain-i-Akbari is its third volume and records the administration, revenue and statistics of Akbar's empire.
e: The Akbarnama has three volumes — the last one, Ain-i-Akbari, is the gazetteer.

q: 'Wings of Fire' is the autobiography of which person?
x: 'Wings of Fire', written with Arun Tiwari and published in 1999, is A. P. J. Abdul Kalam's autobiography covering his life up to 1991.
e: Kalam's other well-known titles: 'Ignited Minds' and 'India 2020'.

q: The novel 'Godan' was written by whom?
x: 'Godan' (1936) is Munshi Premchand's last completed novel; it follows the peasant Hori and is regarded as a classic of Hindi fiction.
e: Godan = 'the gift of a cow' — the wish Hori never manages to fulfil.

q: The Thomas Cup is associated with which sport?
x: The Thomas Cup is the world men's team championship in badminton; the women's equivalent is the Uber Cup. India won the Thomas Cup for the first time in 2022.
e: Badminton team cups: Thomas (men), Uber (women), Sudirman (mixed).

q: Who was the first Indian to win an individual gold medal at the Olympic Games?
x: Abhinav Bindra won gold in the 10 m air rifle at Beijing in 2008 — India's first individual Olympic gold. Neeraj Chopra won the second, in the javelin, in 2021.
e: Bindra 2008 (shooting), Chopra 2021 (javelin).

q: The term 'bully' is used in which sport?
x: 'Bully' is the hockey term for the old way of restarting play, with two opponents tapping sticks over the ball. Modern rules have replaced it in most situations.
e: Hockey words: bully, dribble, penalty corner, short corner.

q: National Sports Day in India is observed on 29 August to mark the birth anniversary of which sportsperson?
x: National Sports Day is held on 29 August, the birthday of hockey player Major Dhyan Chand, who won Olympic golds in 1928, 1932 and 1936. The national sports awards are given on this day.
e: Dhyan Chand was called 'The Wizard'; the Khel Ratna award is now named after him.

q: The headquarters of the International Court of Justice is located in which city?
x: The International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands.
e: The ICJ is the only main UN organ that does not sit in New York.

q: The headquarters of UNESCO is located in which city?
x: UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, has its headquarters in Paris, France.
e: Paris: UNESCO. Rome: FAO. Nairobi: UNEP. Vienna: IAEA.

q: National Science Day is observed in India on 28 February to mark the discovery of which phenomenon?
x: National Science Day marks C. V. Raman's announcement of the Raman effect on 28 February 1928; he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1930.
e: Raman effect = scattering of light with a change of wavelength; 28 February, Nobel 1930.

q: Who was the first woman President of India?
x: Pratibha Patil was President of India from 2007 to 2012 — the first woman to hold the office. Droupadi Murmu, who took office in 2022, is the second.
e: First woman Prime Minister: Indira Gandhi. First woman President: Pratibha Patil.

q: Which is the highest civilian award of India?
x: The Bharat Ratna, instituted in 1954, is India's highest civilian award. The Param Vir Chakra is the highest military gallantry award, not a civilian one.
e: Civilian order: Bharat Ratna, then Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri.

q: Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian to travel to space, flew aboard a spacecraft of which country?
x: Rakesh Sharma flew on the Soviet Soyuz T-11 mission in April 1984 and spent about eight days aboard the Salyut 7 space station.
e: Asked by Indira Gandhi how India looked from space, he answered 'Saare Jahan Se Achcha'.
